attribution.note: Marcus's own words in his Substack post. The reference to the settlement is his own assertion, not a quote of someone else.

semantics.note: The proposition faithfully covers the copyright part of the sentence. The safety-pledge clause is a separate claim and is rightly left out. It is a firm past-tense observation.

contract.note: Reading 'ripped off' as unauthorized acquisition of pirated books is fair and ordinary. It neither requires a liability verdict nor claims that training infringed. A broader reading that includes unlawful training would fail on the fair-use ruling, so the reading matters to the result.

evidence.note: October 2025 court opinion: Anthropic downloaded millions of books from pirate libraries, which was not fair use on the summary-judgment record, and the settlement covers about 482k works. This establishes substantial unauthorized copying.
Settlement notice filed 2025-10-01 confirms an agreed $1.5B fund before the February 2026 post. It also says liability is still disputed, so on its own it does not prove wrongdoing.
June 2025 order: training use was fair use, and the pirated library copies were sent to trial. This bounds the claim without contradicting the acquisition reading.

reviews.rationale: Court records (e1, e3) show Anthropic downloaded millions of pirated books into its library, and the court found this was not fair use on the summary-judgment record. A $1.5B settlement over those works was agreed and filed by October 2025, before the post (e2). There was no final liability verdict and training was held to be fair use. Even so, the plain reading of unauthorized copying on a large scale holds.
